newsitem.title: GERMANY: Building union to protest over east German wages.
newsitem.headline: Building union to protest over east German wages.

text.p: Germany's IG Bau building sector union said on Monday it planned a protest campaign against the unprecedented decision last month by German builders to scrap wage agreements for east German workers.

IG Bau chief Klaus Wiesehuegel told a news briefing that a "huge campaign of information" would go ahead if, as expected, agreed pay increases for east German workers do not show up in their October pay packets.
The union last week said it had filed a legal action seeking to prove that wage agreements could not be dissolved by one party alone.

The agreements, signed earlier this year in March and April, covered wages and training funds and were an attempt to bring conditions in the east of the country more closely in line with those in the west.

But the Hauptverband der Deutschen Bauindustrie sector association said in August that eastern firms were not in a position to finance the agreed increases and that the industry there was in an "emergency situation".

"We need a ruling on this...once and for all," Wiesehuegel told journalists, adding that negotiations for the next round of wage agreements could not begin until the industrial tribunal in Wiesbaden had announced its ruling.

IG Bau reiterated that it had no plans to strike on the issue, at least until the court had announced a decision. The information campaign will seek to explain to construction employees their "financial rights", it added.
The two contracts were to give east German workers a 1.85 percent pay rise from September 1 and lift their salaries to 95 percent of western levels from the current 92 percent.
Terminating the agreements, the industry asociation said that a wage freeze was the only way to even out a competitive imbalance between east and west.

Wages in the German construction sector are currently under severe pressure mainly because of competition from foreign firms employing cheaper labour compounded by a harsh winter last year which contributed to an industry slump.
